pr.title: Administrator: protect saved passwords with DPAPI (1.3)
pr.body:
## Summary

Phase 1.3: the Administrator's saved connection passwords are now **protected with DPAPI for the Windows user**.

They were stored in `%APPDATA%\…\hMailAdmin.exe.config`, AES-encrypted under a key derived from `THIS_KEY_IS_NOT_SECRET`. That key is in the source code, so anyone with a copy of the file could read the server administrator's password.

## Changes

- **`Utilities/Encryption.cs`**:
  - `Encrypt` now writes `dpapi1:<base64>`, a `CryptProtectData` blob for the current user, with entropy of its own. Only that Windows user, on that computer, can unprotect it.
  - `Decrypt` reads both the new format and the old AES values.
  - `CryptProtectData` is called through P/Invoke rather than `ProtectedData`. In .NET 10, `ProtectedData` comes in a separate NuGet package that the installer would also have to ship.
- **`UserSettings.Load`** re-protects any password saved the old way and saves the settings, so the old key is relied on at most once. A password that can't be read either way is left alone and asked for when connecting, as before.

## Tests

`Security.AdministratorSavedPasswords` runs against the **installed** `hMailAdmin.dll`, through reflection, because the Administrator has no test project of its own:

- `TestSavedPasswordIsProtectedWithDpapi`:
  - a saved password is a `dpapi1:` value that reads back unchanged;
  - each protection produces a new blob;
  - a changed blob throws `CryptographicException`.
- `TestPasswordSavedTheOldWayIsRead`: the test builds a value the way earlier versions did (`PasswordDeriveBytes` + AES); it is recognised as the old format and decrypts correctly.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

commit.message:
Administrator: protect saved passwords with DPAPI for the Windows user

The Administrator saved the passwords of its server connections in
hMailAdmin.exe.config AES-encrypted under a key derived from
THIS_KEY_IS_NOT_SECRET, which is in the source code: anyone with the file could
read the server administrator's password.

They are protected with DPAPI now, for the Windows user who saved them, with
entropy of their own: dpapi1:<base64 of the blob>. Only that user on this
computer can unprotect them. CryptProtectData is called directly: .NET has
ProtectedData only in a package of its own, which the installer would have to
ship too.

A password saved the old way is still read, and UserSettings.Load protects it
again and saves the settings, so the old key is relied on once at most. One
that cannot be read either way is left as it is, and asked for when connecting,
as before.

Tests (Security.AdministratorSavedPasswords, on the installed hMailAdmin.dll,
as the Administrator has no tests of its own):
- a saved password is a dpapi1 value that reads back as it was, every
  protection is a new blob, and a changed one does not unprotect;
- a password saved the old way, made the way earlier versions made it, is
  recognised as such and read.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
